Abstract
Data is generated at high volume and speed, creating both challenges and opportunities. Cloud computing has further 
amplified some of these challenges, particularly in terms of storage options, availability of storage locations, and data 
access latency. To simplify data management and avoid the complexities of migrating data between cloud providers, 
most cloud users prefer subscribing to a single provider for hosting their applications and datasets. However, multicloud 
environments mitigate vendor lock-in risks while offering cost benefits and access to specialized services. In this paper, 
we propose an adaptive data placement framework (ADAPT) framework designed to optimize data storage costs and 
enhance data availability in multicloud environments. We approach the selection of optimal storage locations and data 
availability as classification problems. To evaluate our method, we applied four popular machine learning models and 
assessed their performance. Our results indicate that the XGBoost model effectively improves cost efficiency from 6.58% 
to 24.26% and data file availability. We then integrated XGBoost into the ADAPT framework and presented prototype 
results demonstrating its effectiveness.

Cloud storage-based data management is a widely 
studied research area. Broadly, existing works can be cat­
egorized into three main focuses: Optimizing data storage 
costs while enhancing availability [1–11]; Data placement 
strategies [2, 6–11]; and Improving performance, particu­
larly throughput and latency  [10, 12–18]. Many of these 
studies primarily propose algorithms rather than complete, 
easily implementable solution frameworks. Additionally, 
most existing research does not account for user prefer­
ences or restrictions on data storage locations-an aspect our 
approach addresses. Further research is needed to develop 
privacy-aware data management solutions for multicloud 
environments.
1.2  Research context
To bridge this research gap, we propose an adaptive data 
placement framework (called ADAPT). The primary objec­
tives of ADAPT are: i) to minimize data storage costs by 
determining optimal storage locations and ii) to enhance 
data availability, ultimately improving application per­
formance (i.e., latency) in a multicloud environment. Our 
goal is to develop an effective data placement solution that 
enables cloud service users to seamlessly move data across 
cloud platforms while accommodating various user prefer­
ences, such as specific storage location requirements. This 
study is guided by the central research question: How can 
machine learning be leveraged for effective data place­
ment to optimize storage costs and data availability in 
multicloud platforms? The primary research question fur­
ther breaks down into two sub-research questions which are 
cost optimization and performance optimization focused. 
They are:
	
●
How can data placement be optimized to reduce costs 
while considering user storage location preferences?
	
●
How can datasets be effectively prefetched to improve 
data availability?
The ultimate objective of this study is to determine whether 
a prototype can be implemented within a multicloud envi­
ronment to address data placement challenges while opti­
mizing both storage costs and data access latency using 
machine learning (ML) classification algorithms. To explore 
this, we selected four widely used classification models: 
decision tree, random forest, eXtreme Gradient Boosting 
(XGBoost), and Support Vector Machine (SVM). The pro­
totype was developed using Apache Spark and the Spring 
Boot framework, with results formatted in JavaScript object 
notation (JSON). Overall contributions of this work: 
1.	 We propose the ADAPT architecture and provide a 
detailed explanation of its modules.
2.	 We observed effectiveness of the XGBoost model for 
predictive tasks, demonstrating superior accuracy and 
F1 scores compared to decision tree, random forest, and 
SVM.
3.	 We showcase the application of XGBoost in provid­
ing data-driven recommendations for cloud storage 
optimisation. These recommendations include suggest­
ing alternative providers and regions to achieve cost 
savings, while also considering constraints (such as 
allowed migration types and prohibited locations).
4.	 The framework also presents proactive resource man­
agement through file prefetching based on user access 
patterns and geographical locations.
2  Related work
We have broadly categorized existing works into three main 
categories: (i) cost reduction, (ii) performance improve­
ment, and (iii) data sharing.
2.1  Cost reduction
Li et al. proposed a combinatorial method to realize bet­
ter data placement [2]. Vergilio et al. proposed a big data 
stream processing architecture for multicloud computing 
to mitigate the risks of vendor lock-in [3]. Chikhaoui et al. 
addressed the data placement issue by developing a multi-
objective constrained optimization problem focusing on 
data storage, migration and latency costs [6]. [8] propose 
a data placement algorithm to facilitate data processing on 
collaborative cloud platforms. Xu et al. proposed an algo­
rithm to optimize resource usage, energy cost, and latency 
[11]. Wang et al. proposed a genetic algorithm-based data 
placement technique for a multicloud setup [7]. Jiang et al. 
proposed a cost-aware application scheduling algorithm that 
creates an abstraction layer over the compute and storage 
resources to reduce complexity [10], while [5] proposed an 
optimization algorithm to achieve a trade-off between cost 
and data availability to prevent vendor lock-in. Chaudhary 
et al. presented a software-defined networking-based data 
management approach that uses a Bloom filter to optimize 
network bandwidth and data storage cost [18]. Rafique et al.

2.3  Data sharing
Yu et al. addressed the data sharing problem by designing 
a cloud-native distributed object store [14]. Zhang et al. 
proposed a distributed in-memory cache system to manage 
efficiently sharing data with data dependencies [15]. [21] 
shows how to automate scientific workflow execution in 
an edge-cloud platform. Bouhouch et al. proposed a data 
placement strategy to improve workflow execution time by 
reducing the cost reduction associated with data movements 
[9]. In addition, Demchenko et al. proposed data lifecycle 
management for scientific application [20].
In Table 1, we compare the aforementioned works based 
on their research goals, support for multicloud, application 
domains, data management features, and support for non­
functional requirements. For performance-oriented stud­
ies, we identified three primary approaches: data caching 
or prefetching, task scheduling, and a combination of both.
We observed that most previous studies treated cost 
reduction as an optimization problem. However, we address 
cost reduction as a classification problem using ML algo­
rithms. In addition, most studies have proposed theoreti­
cal solutions rather than complete frameworks for cloud 
users. The proposed data management framework, ADAPT, 
optimizes storage costs and latency using ML-driven data 
placement across multicloud environments. It leverages 
multiple ML models for data-driven recommendations. 
ADPAT delivers practical, JSON-formatted results while 
implementing Apache Spark and Spring Boot frameworks.
3  ADAPT: adaptive data placement 
framework
To enable applications to run seamlessly across multi­
cloud infrastructures with reduced data storage costs and 
enhanced performance, we propose the ADAPT framework. 
The proposed framework is designed for cloud service users 
who have access to multiple cloud platforms, including both 
individuals and companies that manage various datasets for 
application execution. These applications can access datas­
ets distributed across different regions within the same CSP 
or across multiple CSPs. In this context, ADAPT serves as 
a data management system capable of handling geographi­
cally distributed datasets. ADAPT is in charge of selecting 
optimal data storage locations and managing runtime data 
transfers. ADAPT manages data sources on behalf of users 
by assigning storage, access, and transfer costs based on 
user data access requirements. The proposed framework 
optimizes data placement and migration by monitoring data 
and virtual machine (VM) access. In addition, it provides 
RESTful APIs to facilitate data migration. ADAPT should 
be operated continuously using the MAPE (Monitoring, 
Analyzing, Planning, and Execution) loop. This allows the 
system to constantly monitor data access and system perfor­
mance, making real-time decisions about data placement. 
ADAPT considers user preferences (such as prohibited stor­
age locations or latency requirements) and platform-specific 
information when determining the most efficient data stor­
age solutions.
3.1  Overview of ADAPT
ADAPT is a modular system consisting of several com­
ponents, each focusing on specific operational aspects to 
achieve common objectives. Figure 1 provides an overview 
of the key modules.
	
●
ADAPT API and Web UI: Provides an interface for 
users and external client applications to interact with 
ADAPT. This includes importing datasets, submitting 
and executing applications, and updating user prefer­
ences and datasets.
	
●
Dataset Import Module: Manages an internal database 
of user datasets, user preferences (e.g., latency require­
ments and prohibited locations), and available data cen­
ter locations from supported CSPs.
	
●
Data Access and Prefetch Module: Handles the data ac­
cess needs of the user application during runtime, main­
taining a cache by prefetching data to improve the per­
formance of the application.

3.3  Interactions of modules
We use a sequence diagram to provide an overview of 
the interactions between the key modules and the entities 
they interact with. The diagram illustrates the sequential 
exchange of data or messages between components over 
time.
3.3.1  Cost optimization
We model this problem as a classification task that takes 
user inputs (related to application and data) and outputs the 
storage location that minimizes storage costs. The model 
must account for user-specific constraints (such as location 
preferences) and support at least three CSPs (i.e., Amazon, 
Google, and Microsoft) that must be located in the Euro­
pean Union. The cost of each storage location is determined 
by the data access cost (sum of read and write costs), data 
storage cost, and latency cost (which is considered only for 
latency-sensitive applications).
As shown in Fig. 3 (left side), the process begins with 
the user’s input, which includes the dataset and other 
preferences. Users can optimize costs using one or more 
datasets. The user interacts with the system through the 
RestHandler interface, which provides RESTful APIs for 
specific functionalities. Once the user’s request is validated, 
the selected datasets are forwarded to the MLClassifierOp­
tLocSelect module, which uses SparkClient to determine 
optimal storage locations. MLClassifierOptLocSelect calls 
thesubmitTask() function (part of SparkClient) to submit 
the task of recommending the best storage locations, based 
on the characteristics of each dataset, to an instance of the 
Apache Spark Server. Prior to task submission, the datasets 
are converted into CSV (comma-separated values) format 
for easier processing. Once the task is submitted, a polling 
process is initiated in the SparkClient to monitor task com­
pletion. After the task is completed, the results are returned 
to MLClassifierOptLocSelect, which then estimates the 
cost and potential savings of placing the data at the recom­
mended location. Finally, the dataset list, recommended 
locations, costs, and estimated savings are sent back to the 
RestHandler, which transforms the results into JSON format 
for presentation to the user. Apache Spark allows the activa­
tion of REST endpoints for task submission.

4.1  Training process
The training script uses a pipeline that begins by convert­
ing string features (e.g., location, storage name) to numeri­
cal representations with StringIndexer. After indexing all 
string-based values of the dataset input features, all dataset 
features are assembled into a feature vector with a Vecto­
rAssembler. The feature vector merges multiple feature 
columns into a single vector column, which simplifies the 
input data format required by ML algorithms. The single 
vector feature, which is the output of VectorAssembler, is 
then subsequently fed into a StandardScaler. The Standard­
Scaler serves the purpose of normalizing or standardizing 
the numerical values of the input features and ensuring that 
all features are treated equally. After data transformations, 
the indexed, vectorized, and scaled input dataset features 
are input to the classifier algorithm. The classifier algorithm 
builds a model that learns from the sample training data of 
the input features and output storage locations. The pipe­
line ends with an IndexToString converter which reverts the 
work of the StringIndexer since the ML models only work 
with numbers, and we require the result in a human-read­
able format that can be easily interpreted and understood. 
The output of the pipeline is a model that can be saved and 
used later for predictions on new data.

3.3.2  Performance optimization
We aim to enhance data access performance (latency) by 
improving data availability through optimal storage loca­
tions for dataset prefetching. The problem is defined by 
factors such as  data proximity to the user,  latency char­
acteristics of nearby data center locations, and  location 
popularity of data files at specific sites. To address the prox­
imity issue, we construct a map of traversable countries in 
a JSON file. After identifying all possible storage locations, 
we determine the expected latency for each location using a 
latency data store in CSV format.
The RestHandler interface receives input from the user 
(as shown on the right side of Fig. 3), including preferences 
and access information. The Application ID identifies the 
specific application and the file access location. The Res­
tHandler interface then forwards the request to the Prefe­
tchOptimizer, which uses SparkClient to submit the request 
to the  Apache Spark Server. Before submission,  Spark­
Client formats the data into CSV format. Once the task is 
submitted, a polling process is initiated in SparkClient to 
check for task completion. The task recommends the opti­
mal location for prefetching a file, as well as other related 
files that the user might access next. By prefetching these 
related files, we aim to reduce data access latencies for the 
user. The results of the recommendation task are written 
to the worker logs of the Apache Spark Server. Once the 
task is confirmed, SparkClient reads the results and returns 
them to PrefetchOptimizer, which then forwards them to the 
calling client through the RestHandler interface. The Rest­
Handler performs additional formatting before returning the 
response as a JSON message to the user.

They include SVM (baseline model), decision trees, random

It is worth noting that the CrossValidator class in the

achieved stratified k-fold cross-validation in three steps: 
first we applied randomSplit() (of PySpark) to each subset

set were then combined to form the final stratified folds. We 
implemented a pipeline to ensure that StandardScaler was 
applied in each fold.
4.3  Error measures
Error measures, or cost functions, are used to quantify the 
difference between predicted and actual values. We used 
two error evaluators. Accuracy which is a common error 
measure used in classification tasks to evaluate model per­
formance. Here, represents the proportion of correctly clas­
sified instances out of all instances in the dataset [23]. F1 is 
used for evaluating the accuracy of the classification model. 
It balances the trade-off between precision and recall by 
computing the harmonic mean of these two metrics.

Similar to the cost training process, the pipeline begins 
with a StringIndexer and ends with an IndexToString trans­
former that converts the predicted numerical values, which 
represent a specific data center location, back into string-
based, human-readable, and interpretable predictions. The 
main difference between cost optimization and performance 
optimization pipelines is that, unlike cost optimization 
pipelines, performance optimization pipelines include an 
additional step for building and retrieving popular related 
files (i.e., top three other files) for any given data file at a 
specific location (for every combination of FileLocation 
and AccessLocation). This step is illustrated as step nine in 
the sequence diagram for performance optimization (refer 
to right side of Fig. 3). To assist with model training and 
performance evaluation (or error measures), two different 
multi-class classification evaluators were employed: accu­
racy, and F1 score (refer to Sect. 4.3 for more). We divided

5.3.3  Models’ performance
From the result (refer to Table 5), we found that all models 
performed reasonably well while predicting the best data 
placement location while considering forbidden data storage 
location preferences, including application type and system 
state information. The cost optimization was an instance of 
a classification problem, where XGBoost was the winner, 
and the baseline model (i.e., SVM) was the worst performer.
We can see that if we combine the predictors not inde­
pendently, but sequentially it performs best (a known fact 
[26] and true for this case). Generally, XGBoost attempts 
to fit new predictors to residual errors created by previous 
predictors and, finally, summarizes predictions from all 
predictors. XGBoost predictors can be selected from deci­
sion trees, regressors, and classifiers. For this task, we have 
selected SparkXGBoostClassifier. It is a PySpark ML esti­
mator that implements the XGBoost classification algorithm 
based on the XGBoost Python library. XGBoost may overfit 
but we have handle the overfitting problem by using k-fold 
cross-validation. In XGBoost, subsequent predictors learn 
from the mistakes of previous predictors, meaning that each 
predictor corrects its predecessor. We expect OptimalLoca­
tion as the outcome, encompassing all ten input features.
Random forest also shows strong performance, while 
decision tree and SVM exhibit lower scores. For decision 
tree and random forest tasks, we employed a suitable clas­
sifier for binary and multi-class labels and both continuous 
and categorical features. For all four classification tasks, 
feature scaling was performed prior to model training. SVM 
was selected as baseline model, in general, it can maxi­
mize predictive accuracy while avoiding overfitting. We 
have used LinearSVC classifier, which is a binary classifier 
that optimizes the Hinge Loss (popularly used for training 
classifiers).

6.3  Implications
Our proposal is a complete, easily implementable solution 
framework (ADAPT), in contrast to many existing works 
that primarily suggest algorithms (refer to Section 2). The 
ADAPT framework have several key implications:
	
●
By facilitating data placement across multiple cloud 
providers, ADAPT directly addresses the risk of vendor 
lock-in. This allows users to leverage the best services 
and pricing from different CSPs without being tied to a 
single provider.
	
●
The Data Access and Prefetch module aims to improve 
data availability and reduce access latency by prefetch­
ing data based on user access patterns and geographical 
locations which can lead to a better user experience. By 
intelligently recommending optimal storage locations 
based on multiple factors, users can reduce their cloud 
6  Discussion and limitation
6.1  Model discussion
The test results indicate that optimizing data placement for 
cost and performance can be framed as a classification prob­
lem. we found that XGBoost excels at both error measures. 
During the execution of XGBoost, we attempted to achieve 
maximum parallelization for faster training process.
In some scenarios, the decision tree can easily interpret a 
small dataset compared to random forest. SVMs can strug­
gle with large feature-based classification problems because 
SVM require solving a quadratic optimization problem. The 
problem becomes computationally expensive as the num­
ber of features increases. In addition, the sparsity of feature 
space can make it difficult to find hyperplanes.
6.2  Applicability
We have developed ADAPT for cloud service users to 
address two key issues.  1. Cost Optimization: ADAPT 
selects optimal data storage locations to reduce costs, 
enhance availability, and minimize vendor lock-in through 
multicloud support. For distributed datasets, the forbidden 
locations feature ensures privacy-aware computing. 2. Data 
Availability and Performance: ADAPT improves access

ADAPT offers cloud service users more control over

6.4  Limitation
Similar to multiple ML projects, we also face a major prob­
lem, i.e., the lack of quality and quantity of data. We have 
diligently combined three sets of data and features, i.e., CSP 
platform-related data, four large public datasets, and Netflix 
data. We also ensured that the sample training data is rep­
resentative of both scenarios and that the findings could be 
generalized. The selected models can be replaced based on 
the data features.
In addition, this study assumed to deal with only hot 
datasets while overlooking cold and archive storage. There 
is also a need to update storage options from various CSP 
sources when is relevant.
7  Conclusion and future work
Cloud platforms are dynamic, and updated features can 
leverage specialized services and reduce data manage­
ment costs. However, vendor lock-in is a critical problem 
in cloud computing ecosystems. Effective and efficient data 
management across different cloud providers to realize the 
best value for money is a complex problem. The proposed 
multicloud ecosystem helps to avoid vendor lock-in.
Overall, the ADAPT framework represents a significant 
step toward more efficient and cost-effective data manage­
ment in multicloud environments. Its emphasis on user 
preferences, the application of ML, and the provision of a 
complete solution framework has important implications for 
reducing vendor lock-in, optimizing costs, and enhancing 
data availability. However, addressing the identified limita­
tions is crucial for realizing the full potential of this work.
In future work, we plan to include more data storage 
features (such as cold and archive storage) and inter-data 
transfer costs between different CSPs. There is also a need 
to develop more sophisticated data collection strategies to 
build more comprehensive and representative datasets for 
training other complex models. Future work will incorpo­
rate monitoring and feedback mechanisms into the frame­
work. In addition, it would be interesting to investigate 
security concerns when handling data from multiple CSPs.

Abstract: Data is generated at high volume and speed, creating both challenges and opportunities. Cloud computing has further amplified some of these challenges, particularly in terms of storage options, availability of storage locations, and data access latency. To simplify data management and avoid the complexities of migrating data between cloud providers, most cloud users prefer subscribing to a single provider for hosting their applications and datasets. However, multicloud environments mitigate vendor lock-in risks while offering cost benefits and access to specialized services. In this paper, we propose an adaptive data placement framework (ADAPT) framework designed to optimize data storage costs and enhance data availability in multicloud environments. We approach the selection of optimal storage locations and data availability as classification problems. To evaluate our method, we applied four popular machine learning models and assessed their performance. Our results indicate that the XGBoost model effectively improves cost efficiency from 6.58% to 24.26% and data file availability. We then integrated XGBoost into the ADAPT framework and presented prototype results demonstrating its effectiveness.
